title: Should you buy the Elitefts SS Yoke bar (instead of its Rogue or Titan counterpart)?
summary: Review of the Elitefts SS Yoke safety squat bar, which he rates the best SSB thanks to its thick pad and easy-to-grip handles. He argues the SSB is not an easier squat but a different, harder movement that pitches you forward; start at about 50% of your max. For good mornings he considers it the only proper option.

claims.claim: The Elitefts SS Yoke bar weighs 60 lb and its sleeves are slightly thinner than an Olympic bar's, so regular collars slide; cheap hardware-store clamps solve it.
Full price is $400, but Elitefts sales bring it to $280-300, around the price of Titan and Rogue SSBs; wait for a sale.
He considers it the best safety squat bar available, mainly because its thick pad means you never feel metal on your shoulders, unlike thin, sliding pads on other SSBs.
The standard handles are fine for most people (he is 6 ft); only very long-armed lifters need the longer handles.
Lifters with a small frame and narrow shoulders may have their elbows hit their thighs with an SSB, cutting squat depth, which is a drawback for ass-to-grass squats.
He uses the SSB for block squats, good mornings and movements where you wrap your arms tightly around the padded bar and yank on it.
The SSB handles solve the shoulder-mobility problem of the high-bar squat, where many powerlifters resort to very wide or false grips.
Because the bar weighs 60 lb, a brand-new or weak lifter may need to ramp up before using it.
The SSB is not an easier squat but a different movement: its camber shifts the load so you cannot squat your straight-bar weight with it.
The SSB pushes you forward and tries to fold you in half; fighting that is what makes it so effective, and using your normal working weight first time will get you stapled.
When starting SSB squats, begin with about 50% of your squat max and ramp up.
SSB squats initially felt strange and slightly injurious on a joint, but the sensation went away with practice.
The SSB is the only way he does good mornings; a straight-bar good morning is really a 'squat morning', not a true good morning.
With a straight bar, people either go high-bar but use little weight for fear of it rolling onto the neck, or go low-bar, which puts the load mid-back and makes the good morning easier.
He did straight-bar good mornings with 245 lb for 12, but with the SSB could not get 135 lb for 12.
